title: Ancient Galaxies Are Way Bigger Than We Thought!
summary:
Have you ever looked at a city skyline and only noticed the tallest skyscrapers? Well, astronomers did something like that with galaxies, and they found out they were missing a lot!

Using the James Webb Space Telescope, scientists looked at nine big, old galaxies that stopped making new stars billions of years ago. They wanted to figure out how many stars were in them. But here's the tricky part: the biggest, brightest stars are easy to see, while smaller, dimmer stars are hidden behind them.

It's like if a galaxy were a city, the bright stars are the skyscrapers you see from far away. But there are tons of little houses hiding between them. Those houses are the small stars, and there are way more of them than anyone thought!

So, these ancient galaxies might be three or four times more massive than scientists first guessed. That's a huge surprise!

One galaxy was especially amazing. It formed less than one and a half billion years after the Big Bang (that's when the universe began), and it could be four times more massive than we thought.

This is a big deal because it changes what we know about how galaxies formed. If these early galaxies have so many small stars, then our models of how galaxies grow need to be updated.

And here's a cool bonus: if there are more stars, there might also be more planets around them! So, the early universe might have had more places for life to start.

Scientists are excited to keep exploring with JWST to learn even more about these mysterious, massive galaxies.
why_it_matters: Learning about ancient galaxies shows how science can change when new tools reveal hidden stars, and it may inspire you to ask big questions about the universe.

background_read: Astronomers once thought the first galaxies were small and simple, but newer tools are changing that picture.
The James Webb Space Telescope (a giant space telescope that can see older and dimmer light than earlier telescopes) was built to look far back in time.
When we look at light from very far away, we are seeing the universe as it was billions of years ago.
Article_Structure: WHO: Astronomers using the James Webb Space Telescope looked at nine big, old galaxies.
WHAT: They found these ancient galaxies might be three or four times more massive than first thought because hidden small stars were missed.
WHERE: The study looked at old galaxies that stopped making new stars billions of years ago in the early universe.
WHY: This changes scientific models of how galaxies formed and suggests the early universe may have had more places for life.

perspectives.description: Astronomers are excited because this discovery gives them a better idea of how galaxies grew and could mean more places for life began in the early universe.
Some scientists may feel cautious because the old models of galaxy growth were incomplete, so the new findings need to be checked with more galaxies.
Researchers want to use JWST to study more ancient galaxies and see whether this pattern of hidden small stars is common.
